help.text: The wallet's message definitions cover Aion, Algorand, Aptos, BNB Beacon Chain, BNB Greenfield, Bitcoin, Cardano, Cosmos SDK chains, Decred, EOS, Ethereum and EVM chains, Everscale, FIO, Filecoin, Harmony, Hedera, ICON, IOST, Internet Computer, IoTeX, MultiversX, NEAR, NULS, Nano, Nebulas, Neo, Nervos CKB, Nimiq, Oasis, Ontology, Polkadot and Substrate chains, Polymesh, Solana, Stellar, Sui, TON, Tezos, Theta, Tron, VeChain, XRP Ledger, Zcash (transparent), æternity. These chains authorize transactions with BLS12-381, ECDSA, Ed25519, Schnorr (BIP-340), sr25519, which Shor's algorithm breaks on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. A wallet cannot move a chain to post-quantum signatures on its own: the chain has to adopt a scheme first. Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them. Keep the signing layer crypto-agile per chain (algorithm identifiers in messages and storage, room for larger keys and signatures) and track each chain's post-quantum proposals, so that a new scheme can be added when a chain activates it. This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Chains are recognized from the names of the message definitions (.proto files and packages); the schemes are the chains' documented account signatures, not an analysis of the wallet's signing code.
